NOT adding a second route. No /api/run/<id>. Query parameters on /api/graph, because an old server ignores an unknown parameter and returns something correct, while an unknown path returns a text/plain 404 the client would have to special-case.
NOT prefetching. No neighbour prefetch, no speculative load, no depth fetched for an active run that is not selected. Watching a second run costs one click and one request.
NOT changing collect_activity's 40-event tail, ACTIVE_STATUSES, WEDGED_SECS, WAITING_ON_A_HUMAN, or the 4s interval.

architect.rationale:
SHAPE. Single-loop, three ordered slices. A disjoint partition DOES exist on paper --
s1 owns fleetview/CLAUDE.md, s2 owns fleetview/serve.py, s3 owns fleetview/index.html +
fleetview/test.js, and no file is touched twice -- so the diamond's file test passes. I am
declining it anyway, for two reasons that the file test cannot see. (1) A real artifact flows
s2 -> s3: the wire contract. s3's client cache, its per-URL ETag map and roughly a dozen new
fixtures ENCODE the exact response shapes s2 emits. Two builders coding to a written contract
in parallel, neither able to run the other half, produce a field-name drift that only the
integrator discovers -- the weakest place in the graph to discover it. Under a diamond that
edge is still real, so it would be a sequence wearing a diamond's clothes. (2) The deliverable
of this run is a single end-to-end number, and no slice can prove it alone. In a sequence,
s3's done_when can be a live measurement against the server s2 already landed; in a diamond
that check has nowhere to live but the integrator, which is where evidence goes to be assumed.
Sizing agrees: s2 is roughly a fifth of the work, so fanning out buys almost nothing, and s1
is the human-gate deliverable -- approved BEFORE code is written, not built beside it.

READING OF THE GOAL, and the one I am rejecting. "Stop shipping every run in full" has two
readings: (a) ship every run but only its light row, and fetch depth per run on demand; (b)
ship the most recent N runs in full and older ones on demand. I recommend (a) and reject (b).
The split must be by DEPTH, not by COUNT. Truncating the list breaks four things at once:
anyRunActive() (index.html:1513) stops seeing a background run and auto-refresh dies;
buildAnonMap() (index.html:369) stops learning an old run's app id and Anonymize silently
prints "App ?" over a real name it should have redacted -- a safety feature failing quietly;
matchesFilter() can no longer find what the search box exists for; and every deep link into
history breaks. Depth-splitting costs none of that, which is why the answers to Q6 and to the
anonymize constraint below come out easy.

WHY OVERTURNING THE PREVIOUS REFUSAL IS NOW RIGHT, and not merely authorized. The
2026-09-04-fleetview-payload architect refused the split, and its reasoning was sound on the
facts it had. Three things have changed, and its own text names two of them.
  1. It argued "the split needs 304 to be good; 304 does not need the split," and it was
     right. 304 now exists. The split is being built ON that mechanism rather than instead of
     it, which is exactly the order that refusal implied. The two are complements: 304
     collapses the UNCHANGED poll to zero bytes, the split collapses the CHANGED poll, and
     neither reaches the other's case.
  2. It booked an explicit revisit at ~40 runs or ~2 MB and named the amendment as the thing
     that must come first. That is not a permanent refusal, it is a sequenced one, and this
     run is doing what it said to do -- amendment first, at the gate, verbatim.
  3. The refusal's sharpest technical objection is the one the scout re-found as the
     PLAN-KILLER: the wedged signal needs _activity recency for EVERY run, and _activity is
     3-4 KB per run. That is why the split looked like it would silently cost a signal. The
     orchestrator has since measured it away -- a light row CARRYING an _activity_last
     timestamp is 5,004 B for the whole list, 0.7% of runs[]. A cost estimated at 3-4 KB per
     run turns out to be ~30 bytes per run. The refusal was reasoning about a plan-killer that
     measurement dissolved; that, not the authorization, is why the answer changes.
  What I am NOT claiming: that the refusal was wrong to ship 304 first. It was right, and the
  savings on an idle fleet are still 304's, not this run's.

THE PRIZE IS THE ACTIVE CASE, so the design starts there. 304 already makes an unchanged poll
free, so the split's marginal value on a quiet fleet is bounded above by roughly zero. The
whole point is the poll where the ETag necessarily misses because a node is writing. Measured:
idle or active-run-not-selected 98.4% saved; active-run-SELECTED 73.0%. The design below adds
one thing to that second number -- the row signature in Q5 -- which lets even a selected active
run skip its own detail fetch on any poll where nothing in that run actually moved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q1. ENDPOINT SHAPE. One endpoint. Additive query parameters on /api/graph. No new route.

  GET /api/graph?fleet=F              -> UNCHANGED. Full payload, every run in full.
  GET /api/graph?fleet=F&runs=light   -> the same payload with runs[] replaced by light rows,
                                         plus a top-level "runs_mode": "light".
  GET /api/graph?fleet=F&run=<id>     -> a detail envelope:
      {generated, active_fleet_id, runs_mode: "detail", run_id: "<id>", run: {...full run...}}

The full payload stays the DEFAULT, and that single choice is the entire compatibility story.
It is free in both directions, in the same style the ETag already uses:
  - OLD client, NEW server: the old page sends neither new parameter, gets the identical bytes
    it got yesterday, and cannot tell anything changed. This is the case that actually happens
    -- a browser tab left open across a `git pull` and a serve.py restart.
  - NEW client, OLD server: the page sends `runs=light`; an old server ignores an unknown query
    value and returns the full payload. The client sees no `runs_mode`, concludes "this server
    does not split", and renders from the full runs[] exactly as today -- large but correct.
    Likewise `run=<id>`: an old server returns the full payload, the client sees no `run` key,
    finds the run inside runs[] and uses it. Zero savings, zero breakage, and no version
    negotiation anywhere.
The client rule is one line: `d.run ? d.run : (d.runs||[]).find(byId)`. Absence degrades to the
old path; it never crashes. That satisfies "a missing or malformed input renders as a visible
state, never as a crash" (CLAUDE.md:173) in both directions.

REJECTED: a second route (/api/run/<id>). Against an old server it returns the text/plain 404
at serve.py:485, which the client must special-case -- and a special case is exactly where
"renders as a visible state" goes to die. An old server ignores an unknown query parameter; it
cannot ignore an unknown path.

SERVER-SIDE REQUIREMENTS on the detail mode, all testable:
  - The run id names a directory. It must NEVER be joined onto runs_dir directly. Resolve it by
    exact name match against the listing collect_runs() already walks, and reject anything else.
    `?run=../../../etc/passwd` must 404, not read. This server ships local filesystem paths in
    its payload and binds 127.0.0.1 precisely because that content is sensitive.
  - An unknown id returns 404 with a JSON body {"error": ..., "run_id": ...}, not the
    text/plain 404, so the client can render a stated "not in this fleet" pane.
  - NO SERVER STATE, and this design does not strain that sentence at all: the detail is
    assembled from disk per request by the same collect_runs() code path filtered to one
    directory, the ETag is recomputed per request, and every cache introduced here lives in the
    browser tab. "There is no cache to invalidate and no state held between requests"
    (CLAUDE.md:33) survives literally. The previous run refused a change on exactly this
    ground; this one does not go near it.

Q2. THE WEDGED SIGNAL. The orchestrator's measurement is confirmed, with one addition.
The light row carries `_activity_last`: one number, defined as EXACTLY what activityAgeSecs()
(index.html:457-465) would compute from the full _activity -- the max over agents[].last AND
tail[].t, not just agents[].last. That definition is the correctness condition and it is
directly testable: wedgedFor() on a light row must equal wedgedFor() on the same run's detail.
activityAgeSecs() gains a fallback and loses nothing: prefer `run._activity` when present (so
every existing wedged test passes unchanged), else `run._activity_last`, else null. A fleet
with no heartbeat still has one clock and still claims nothing. The wedged pill therefore
renders from the run LIST's own data, at ~30 B/run.
THE ADDITION, which is not about wedged at all: the row also carries `_activity_n` -- the event
count collect_activity() already computes as `total`, ~10 B. It exists for cache invalidation,
and it closes a real hole. _activity_last is a timestamp; two events appended within the same
float tick leave it unchanged while the tail moves. A cache invalidated on _activity_last alone
would then show a FROZEN activity lane on a live run, indefinitely -- the single failure mode
this app exists to prevent. Ten bytes a run to make invalidation exact rather than probabilistic
is the right trade. If the human wants the row smaller, this is the field to cut, and cutting it
is a knowing acceptance of a rare permanently-stale lane.

THE LIGHT ROW, in full (flat fields only -- see below):
  run_id, goal, app, status, approved_by_human, _path, _mtime,
  _activity_last, _activity_n, _shape, _n_slices, _n_rejects, _light: true
  plus _error for an unreadable run, preserving serve.py:231-234's visible-error row.
NO NESTED OBJECTS, deliberately. renderRunList() reads r.architect.shape (index.html:1108), so
the cheap move is to ship a stub `architect: {shape}`. Do not. A half-populated `architect` is
precisely the scout's risk 5 -- partial objects flowing into code that expects whole ones, where
`run.architect.plan` reads undefined and renders an EMPTY slice list instead of a loading state.
A flat `_shape` cannot be mistaken for the real key. `_light: true` is the marker any code can
test to ask "is this the whole run?", which is the defensive check the scout found missing
everywhere. `_n_slices` and `_n_rejects` are display-only: they let the detail HEADER render
complete on click so pills do not pop in when the depth lands.
Consequences of splitting by depth: buildAnonMap() needs only `app` from every run and every run
is in the list, so Anonymize keeps working with no change; anyRunActive() needs only `status`,
present for every run; matchesFilter() needs run_id/goal/app/status, all present. None of those
three functions change.

Q3. ETAG WITH TWO RESPONSES. Two independent fixes; both are needed.
  CLIENT: `lastEtag` (a single var) becomes `etags`, a map keyed by the EXACT request URL --
  which already contains fleet, mode and run id, so no key can collide with another. Only the
  silent poll sends If-None-Match, unchanged (index.html:1600); Refresh and a fleet switch still
  send none and still force a 200. THE INVARIANT THAT PREVENTS THE WORST BUG HERE:
  **an ETag and the body it describes are stored together and discarded together, always.** Keep
  an ETag whose cached body was dropped and the next 304 arrives with no body and nothing to
  fall back on -- a blank pane no error path covers. Every cache drop in Q4 drops its ETag in
  the same statement.
  SERVER: the guarantee at serve.py:460-462 must be re-earned for the new responses, not
  assumed. It holds today because fleet, fleets and active_fleet_id are inside the hashed
  content. A bare run object contains no fleet id, and two fleets can hold a run directory with
  the same id and a byte-identical state.json (a copied run), so a detail ETag computed over the
  run alone could legitimately match across fleets -- a false 304 showing fleet A's run under
  fleet B. Therefore the detail envelope must carry `active_fleet_id` and `run_id` INSIDE the
  hashed content, and `runs_mode` goes inside the hashed content of both new responses.
  Consequence, worth stating as a property: a light response's ETag can never equal a full
  response's, and one fleet's can never equal another's, AT THE SERVER -- so the client's
  per-URL keying is a second line of defence rather than the only one. Hashing itself is
  untouched: SHA-256 over the serialization with `generated` popped (serve.py:382-398),
  content-derived, never mtime, for the reason CLAUDE.md:52-54 already gives.

Q4. CACHING AND INVALIDATION. Client-side only: `runCache[run_id] = {run, etag, sig}` where
  sig = _mtime + "|" + _activity_last + "|" + _activity_n, taken from the light row the detail
  was fetched against. Discard rules, all of them:
  1. FLEET SWITCH -- clear the ENTIRE cache and its ETags. Not re-key by fleet: clear. The
     existing constraint (CLAUDE.md:233) says a run id from one fleet is meaningless in another;
     the same-id-different-fleet collision is the scout's unknown 4; and clearing is one
     statement that is provably correct where keying is a thing to get subtly wrong later.
  2. THE ROW MOVED -- on every list response, for each cached run compare the fresh row's sig to
     the stored one. Differ -> drop that entry and its ETag. This is how you know it moved:
     _mtime catches a node writing state.json, _activity_n catches the heartbeat appending, and
     _activity_last is belt and braces.
  3. THE RUN VANISHED from the light list (archived, deleted) -> drop it.
  4. REFRESH -- clear the whole cache. Refresh means "rebuild the page now", and it already
     forces a 200 by sending no If-None-Match; a cache surviving it would make the button a lie.
     This preserves the existing semantic rather than adding a new one.
  No time-based expiry. It is a localhost viewer polling every 4s: staleness is bounded by the
  poll, and a TTL would only add a second, weaker answer to a question rule 2 answers exactly.

Q5. THE ACTIVE-RUN POLL. The 4s poll fetches THE LIGHT LIST ONLY -- one request, always, the
  same URL every time, conditional exactly as today. It never fetches a detail directly. What it
  does instead is apply rule 2: if the fresh list shows the SELECTED run's sig changed, the
  list's completion handler issues exactly one detail fetch for that run. So:
    - active run NOT selected: list only. ~5 KB against 757 KB -- the 98.4% figure.
    - active run IS selected AND it moved: list + that one detail -- the 73.0% figure.
    - active run IS selected and it did NOT move this tick: LIST ONLY. This is the case the raw
      numbers miss and the signature buys: a selected run whose node is thinking without writing
      state.json or appending a heartbeat event costs 5 KB, not 197 KB. It is also why
      _activity_n has to be exact -- it is the only thing standing between "correctly skipped"
      and "silently frozen".
    - a run that is active but NOT selected never has its detail fetched at all. Depth is
      fetched for the selected run and nothing else: no prefetch, no watching two runs at once.
      Watching a second run is a click, and a click costs one request.
  Ordering: the list response is applied first and the detail is issued from its completion
  handler, never concurrently, so a detail is always fetched against a sig the client has
  already seen.

Q6. DEEP LINKS. Easy, because the list is complete -- every run id that exists is in runs[],
  light or not. Three cases, and the middle one is where the design earns it:
    - the hash names NO run -> currentRun() falls back to runs[0] exactly as today
      (index.html:1124). Unchanged.
    - the hash names a run that IS in the list -> paint its header from the light row
      immediately, show the loading state where the depth will land, fetch one detail. Never
      blank, never a wrong run.
    - the hash names a run that is NOT in the list -> render a stated "run <id> is not in this
      fleet" pane. It must NOT fall back to runs[0].
  That last case changes existing behaviour, and I am flagging it rather than smuggling it in:
  today an unknown id silently redirects to runs[0] (the scout's risk 6). Under a split that
  becomes strictly more dangerous, because a deep link that shows the wrong run's graph while
  the URL names another is worse than one that says it cannot find it. The fallback survives
  only where it is honest -- when nothing was asked for.
  popstate keeps its current shape (re-apply the hash, no refetch unless the FLEET differs,
  index.html:1497-1509) with one addition: after re-applying, if the newly selected run has no
  cached detail, issue the same single detail fetch a click would. Same code path, so there is
  one way to load depth rather than two.

Q7. FAILURE AND LATENCY.
  BETWEEN CLICK AND ARRIVAL: the header panel paints synchronously from the light row --
  run_id, status pill, app, shape, slice count, reject count, gate pill, "state written N ago"
  and the wedged pill -- so everything the run LIST could tell you is on screen with no network
  at all. Below it, in place of the work graph, the slices and the activity lane, one stated
  "loading run detail..." panel. The pane is never blank, and never shows a previous run's graph
  under a new run's title.
  DETAIL FETCH 404s (the run was deleted between the list and the click): a stated banner inside
  the detail pane, header still rendered. Not a crash, not a redirect.
  DETAIL FETCH FAILS (the server died mid-flight): a stated banner inside the detail pane, and a
  retry on the next poll that still finds the run listed.
  THE RULE THAT PROTECTS THE POLL, and the one a reviewer should check hardest: the detail fetch
  lives on its own promise chain that can call neither scheduleAutoRefresh() nor showConnError()
  nor clearConnError(). load() alone owns the timer and the banner. This is the bug that has
  already landed twice -- index.html:1517-1524 is the scar tissue -- and its failure is silent:
  the livedot stays lit while the poll is dead. If the server really is gone, the next 4s poll
  fails inside load() and raises the banner through the path that already exists and already
  reschedules on failure (index.html:1656-1660). Nothing about that path changes.
  OVERLAPPING DETAIL FETCHES (click A, then B before A lands): stamp each detail request with
  its run id and DROP a response whose run id is no longer selectedRun. Otherwise a slow
  response for A paints over B -- the same class of bug as a false 304.
